research.selfAudit: I verified every mechanism in source rather than trusting the reviewers; six of the thirty-five findings did not survive intact and I have said so rather than ratifying the set. Specific corrections I am making against reviewers: (a) RENDER-2's harm text says a large FINITE seed 'likewise never decays' — false, mix() is a lerp and with attackAlpha 0.6 / releaseAlpha 0.85 (AppConfig.swift:143-144) a finite seed converges in one or two frames; only NaN and Inf are absorbing, which is still enough to carry the finding. (b) RENDER-2's belt-and-braces fix proposes `replace(region:)` to zero the textures — that is illegal on a `.private` MTLTexture (replaceRegion requires .shared/.managed); the correct zeroing idioms are a blit copy from a zeroed MTLBuffer or a one-shot render pass with loadAction .clear, and the historyValid uniform should be the primary fix regardless. (c) RENDER-8's sub-claim that the existing test exercises only the equal-stride fast path is probably wrong — the source is created with nil attributes (no IOSurface) while the copy is created WITH kCVPixelBufferIOSurfacePropertiesKey, so their bytesPerRow almost certainly differ and the per-row path does run; the finding's real content (the planar branch that carries capturedImage has zero coverage) is untouched by this. (d) RENDER-5's cost arithmetic assumes 1920x1440 survives the picker, but pickVideoFormat prefers SMALLEST area at the winning fps (GeoARSessionManager.swift:698-701), so on any device that also exposes 1280x720 at the same fps the copy is ~1.38 MB, not 4.15 MB; and an IOSurface-backed CVPixelBufferCreate is nearer 100-300 us than the claimed 0.3-1.0 ms. The defect (unpooled per-call allocation + full-resolution memcpy synchronously on the main actor for pixels Vision immediately scales to ~518x518) stands; the number does not. (e) RENDER-1's proposed remedy ordering is right and I am NOT endorsing a reflexive move to install-once: ADR-035's measurement is a real, documented heat cost of attaching a postProcess callback (RealityKit switches to an offscreen render + full-screen copy the moment the slot is non-nil), and the reviewer's own note that the measurement predates the shader early-out is a reason to re-measure, not a reason to assume it is stale. (f) ARPCFG-5 partially re-litigates ADR-034's explicit written decision ('target-fps formats only, smallest resolution >= 720p, else keep ARKit's default') without new device evidence that any iOS-17-capable handset actually lacks an in-band format at or below 30 fps; I have marked it PARTIAL and asked for the instrumentation to answer that before the policy changes. What I could NOT verify and am flagging as open: I cannot run on device, so every timing number in this review (pipeline compile duration, copy cost, .utility hop latency, TSan outcome for the renderCallbacks store) is an argument from the platform contract, not a measurement — the RENDER-1 TSan harness and the RENDER-5 XCTClockMetric budget are the two that must actually be run before their fixes are sized. I also could not verify ARCore's documented lifetime contract for GARStreetscapeGeometry.mesh vertex buffers read off the main thread (GeospatialEngine.swift:443-451 retains the geometry and asserts this is sufficient); retaining the owning object is the correct-by-construction reading and I found no counter-evidence, but it is an assumption the build makes and no test pins. Finally, I merged rather than padded: ARPCFG-3 with STATE-2, ARPCFG-7 with FLOW-8, STATE-1 with FLOW-5, STATE-7 with FLOW-3, RENDER-5 with RENDER-6, RENDER-3 with RENDER-7 — six pairs where two lenses found the same defect from different angles, and the convergence is itself evidence.
research.shipVerdict: NOT production-grade for the Wave D charter. Wave D genuinely closed ARP-7 (the RealityKit resource-creation-off-main / scene-mutation-on-main split at GeospatialEngine.swift:445-467 is correct and complete), the ARP-12 direction the researcher corrected (MidFieldDepthEstimator.swift:151-156 copies out and never retains the ARFrame; SemanticOcclusionPass.swift:391 flushes once per frame — and the flush is verifiably safe against the retained wrapper array, since CVMetalTextureCacheFlush only recycles entries with no external reference and Metal independently retains encoder-bound textures for the command buffer's life), the transit legs of ARP-8, the gesture-identity half of SWE-5, and the mechanism of SWE-10. Those are real, and the perceptionPlan/pickVideoFormat pure-function extractions are the right industrial shape. But four blockers stand between this build and the wave's own bars, and three of them were INTRODUCED by Wave D fixes: (1) BRIEF hard bar 'zero draw-over-known-front-surface frames' fails deterministically — the occlusionActive migration from static capability to live state was applied to one of its two consumers and not the other, so a window-mode exit taken while reconstruction is momentarily shed removes .occlusion from sceneUnderstanding permanently for the session while the session keeps paying full LiDAR meshing watts and the HUD chip asserts the opposite (GeoARSessionManager.swift:1032 vs :1119 vs :1372; pre-Wave-D line 678 was `occlusionActive = occlusionCapable`, a device constant, which made the same guard correct). Minimum to ship: fix ARPCFG-3/STATE-2, RENDER-2, ARPCFG-1, STATE-1/FLOW-5 and FLOW-1 (with RSCH-1), land the RENDER-1 dwell floor, and re-run FT-28/FT-31 — because RENDER-3, RENDER-6 and ARPCFG-1 all produce fps sawtooth or heat that is indistinguishable from thermal throttling in the current instrumentation, the existing heat traces cannot adjudicate the fixes until they are in.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified line-by-line and this is the strongest finding in the set. ensureMatteTextures (SemanticOcclusionPass.swift:441-450) creates both r16Float textures with storageMode = .private and writes nothing; matteIndex = 0; encode binds matteTextures[matteIndex] at index 7 (366) and the kernel reads it unconditionally as the EMA history — SemanticMatte.metal:235 `float previous = previousMatte.read(gid).r;` then 237 `mix(previous, matte, alpha)` and 238 writes the result back. Metal's contract is explicit that the contents of a newly created texture are undefined, and Metal recycles allocations inside the process without zeroing, so this is not a first-launch-only concern. The absorption argument holds for exactly the cases that matter: mix(NaN, m, a) = NaN forever and `if (smoothed > 0.01)` (240) is false for NaN, so that pixel's occlusion is permanently dead; (1-a)*Inf + a*m = Inf, so Inf is absorbing too, and half(smoothed) saturates at 249 producing a garbage composite weight. Density matters here — any 16-bit word whose top five exponent bits are set decodes to Inf or NaN, i.e. ~1/16 of uniformly random patterns, which turns 'undefined memory' into a speckled few-percent of the frame rather than a rare event. The ping-pong does not heal it: frame 1 writes mix(uninit[0], matte) into texture[1], so the poison propagates into the initialized buffer on the very first encode. Fast-math is a real aggravator, not a rhetorical one — Metal compiles with fast math enabled by default, under which NaN/Inf operands are outside the defined domain, so a shader-side isfinite() guard may be folded away (note the codebase already leans on isfinite at 217 for a different purpose). verdicts.industrialSolution: Primary fix, three lines and fast-math-proof: add `var historyValid: Float` to MatteUniforms (SemanticOcclusionPass.swift:88-125 and the mirrored struct at SemanticMatte.metal:14-44), set it to 0 on the first encode after ensureMatteTextures allocates and 1 thereafter, and change line 235 to `float previous = (uniforms.historyValid > 0.5) ? previousMatte.read(gid).r : matte;`. This is arithmetic-free selection, so no fast-math assumption can defeat it, and it also removes the visible three-frame EMA ramp after every resize. Belt (do it, but as the secondary): zero both textures at allocation with a blit copy from a zeroed MTLBuffer, or a one-shot render pass with loadAction .clear — NOT replace(region:), which requires .shared/.managed storage and will assert on this descriptor. verdicts.reasoning: Mechanism CONFIRMED, magnitude REFUTED. Verified: every CVMetalTextureCacheFlush call site is inside encode (SemanticOcclusionPass.swift:290, 300, 391); setCallbacksActive (163-180) neither flushes nor clears inFlightTextures; uninstall (182-191) nils pipeline and empties matteTextures but never flushes and never nils textureCache — and uninstall is dead code anyway, so the live gap is setCallbacksActive(false). The platform premise is correct and is exactly why Apple's idiom is a per-frame flush: CVMetalTextureCache retains the backing of every buffer it has wrapped, and CVMetalTextureCacheFlush performs the internal recycling that releases entries no longer externally referenced. So when encode stops, recycling stops. Where the finding overreaches is the size of the pin. At the moment of detach the last successful encode has ALREADY flushed at 391, so the only entries surviving are that frame's, which were still externally referenced by the `retained` array at flush time; once the command buffer completes they become unreferenced but unrecycled. That is one capturedImage IOSurface (Y and CbCr are two planes of the SAME surface, not two surfaces), plus segmentation and sceneDepth only if person occlusion happened to be on that frame — realistically one to three surfaces, not a pool. Calling that 'sustained pressure on ARKit's small capture pool producing an fps sawtooth for minutes of walking' is not supported; ARKit's capture pool depth is undocumented but a one-to-three-surface pin is hygiene, not exhaustion. It is still a real leak, it is trivially fixable, and it deserves closing because the detached state IS the app's designed steady state per ADR-035 — I would ship it at LOW/MEDIUM, not MEDIUM.

verdicts.reasoning: Defect CONFIRMED, arithmetic REFUTED. Verified: GeoARSessionManager is @MainActor (line 25) and midDepth.update(frame:hz:) is called from frameUpdate (2282), so both Self.copyPixelBuffer calls at MidFieldDepthEstimator.swift:151-152 execute synchronously on the main actor before the queue.async hop at 158. Each does a fresh CVPixelBufferCreate with IOSurface backing (208-213) — there is no CVPixelBufferPool anywhere in the file — followed by a full memcpy of every plane (221-250), and the result is handed to VNImageRequestHandler (173) with imageCropAndScaleOption = .scaleFill (170), which immediately scales to the Depth Anything V2 Small input; the fit itself samples a normalized 28x20 grid (309-332) and is resolution-agnostic. That is a textbook violation of Apple's own CoreVideo guidance: for repeated per-frame allocations you use a CVPixelBufferPool, because CVPixelBufferCreate with IOSurface properties is a kernel round trip plus a fresh mapping whose first touch faults, and the pool exists specifically to recycle both. Where the finding overreaches: it asserts the surviving format on A17-class hardware is 1920x1440@30 and therefore ~4.15 MB per copy. pickVideoFormat prefers highest fps <= target and then SMALLEST area (GeoARSessionManager.swift:698-701), so on any device that also exposes 1280x720 at the same fps the input is ~1.38 MB; the winning format is device-list-dependent and nobody on this team has dumped supportedVideoFormats. The direction and the fix are right; the budget must come from an instrument, not from arithmetic.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Build one pooled downscaler and use it for BOTH consumers (this is also the RENDER-6 fix, so build it once): a single CVPixelBufferPool sized to the model input (518x518 or 392x392, kCVPixelBufferIOSurfacePropertiesKey set, pool depth 3) plus vImageScale_CbCr8/vImageScale_Planar8 or a vImageConvert_420Yp8_CbCr8ToARGB8888 into the pooled buffer. That removes the per-call IOSurface allocation entirely and cuts copied bytes by roughly 20x, and CVPixelBufferPool's whole purpose is that recycled buffers skip the kernel round trip and the first-touch faults. Keep the LiDAR copy (256x192 Float32, ~196 KB) but pool it too. Keep copyPixelBuffer as the general-purpose helper — it is bounds-correct on both branches, I re-derived the arithmetic — just stop calling it at full camera resolution on the main actor. Tests: testInferenceInputIsPooledAndDownscaled (100 calls with a 1920x1440 biplanar source; assert returned dimensions <= model input, that the number of DISTINCT IOSurface identities across 100 calls is <= pool depth, and an XCTClockMetric total under budget) and testMidDepthUpdateMainThreadCostBudget (device XCTClockMetric over ONLY the synchronous prefix before line 158). Set that budget from a measured baseline on the real device's real chosen format — do not hard-code 0.5 ms from this review's arithmetic; measure first, then pin.

verdicts.reasoning: The charter asked for judgment on this trade and the trade as built is backwards. Verified: PersonSentinel.update takes ARKit's frame.capturedImage by reference from GeoARSessionManager.swift:2249 and captures it in the queue.async closure (PersonSentinel.swift:38-68); the buffer is released only when that closure returns, after handler.perform([request]) at 62. The busy flag (30-36, 40-44) does correctly bound this to one buffer at a time — that half of the build's justification is sound and I credit it. What is not sound is the stated bound. The build's '~10-30 ms hold' is the Vision inference time; the actual hold is queue-hop latency PLUS inference, and the queue is qos: .utility (13). Apple's QoS contract is explicit that utility-class work is the tier the system deprioritizes under CPU contention and, critically, that the system throttles background/utility work when the device is under thermal pressure — which is exactly the state in which ARKit's capture pool is least able to spare a slot. So the hold duration grows precisely when the cost of holding grows. The asymmetry is the tell: MidFieldDepthEstimator, which now COPIES and therefore holds nothing, runs on .userInitiated (MidFieldDepthEstimator.swift:86); the sentinel, which does NOT copy and therefore pins an ARKit surface for the whole hop plus inference, runs on the queue most likely to be starved. verdicts.industrialSolution: Feed the sentinel the same pooled downscaled buffer built for RENDER-5 — a ~512x384 luma or BGRA pooled buffer is ample for upper-body human rectangles — so the copy costs tens of microseconds and ARKit's buffer is released before update() returns. That converts an unbounded, thermally-coupled hold into a bounded one and makes the 'single-buffer, bounded' claim true by construction rather than by assertion. If the copy is rejected on cost grounds, the minimum is to raise the queue to .userInitiated to match the estimator and to instrument the hold: stamp the enqueue time, measure enqueue-to-release, and emit it to metricsLog so FT-28/FT-31 can actually see it. Note the orientation handling at 59-61 (.right) is correct and must survive the downscale — a pooled BGRA/luma buffer keeps the same sensor frame, so pass .right unchanged. Test: testSentinelReleasesCaptureBufferBeforeInferenceCompletes — inject the Vision perform step behind a seam whose double blocks on a semaphore for 500 ms (rule 6: reproduce production's suspension), note the source buffer's IOSurface use count, call update, drop the caller's reference, and assert the count returns to baseline BEFORE the semaphore is signalled. Fails today by construction. Add a second case under real .utility with N spinning threads to measure the hop latency the 'bounded 10-30 ms' claim omits.

I confirmed the governor scenario: PowerGovernor.evaluate (PowerGovernor.swift:58-66) returns .full whenever contentInView and nearestRenderedDistance < 60, and its documented thermal policy is that .serious does NOT demote (70-76), so tier stays .full at thermal .serious while the consumer has already shed itself on !thermalSerious. Request path: setPerception (748-758) → makeConfiguration (628-631) inserts .sceneDepth. Platform contract: ARKit's scene depth is a LiDAR + machine-learning fusion that ARKit computes only when .sceneDepth is present in frameSemantics — Apple documents it as one of the costliest frame semantics and the reason the API is opt-in per configuration. So a drop rendered 10 m ahead with no person in frame requests and runs that pipeline for the entire session with `useful` false on every single frame, and midDepth.update is never called (only feed.invalidate at 2283-2285). That is ADR-033's premise inverted and it is the same request-outlives-use shape the item's own comment at 1157-1160 claims retired. The 4-5 m band is crossed in about two seconds of walking while the visibility radius is 2 km (AppConfig.swift:159), so the leaking case is the normal case.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Make one pure function be provably both the request and the use. (1) Extract the consumer predicate verbatim from frameUpdate:2269-2277 as `nonisolated static func midFieldUseful(distances: [Float], pedestrian: Bool, thermalSerious: Bool, fullTier: Bool) -> Bool` and have frameUpdate call it — no inline copy left behind. (2) Replace the plan's `anyContentBeyondMidMin: Bool` parameter with `midFieldServiceable: Bool`, computed in updatePowerTier from the SAME band expression (d > midDepthMinContentDistance && d < midDepthLiDARBandMax * midDepthSupportMargin), and add `thermalSerious: Bool` to perceptionPlan's signature so the depth term reads `... && midFieldServiceable && fullTier && pedestrian && !thermalSerious`. (3) Then the coupling has a test that cannot drift: testEveryRequestedDepthFrameHasAMidFieldConsumer — for each distance in [4.5, 6, 10, 50, 300, 1900] x thermalSerious in [false, true] with personLikely false, assert perceptionPlan(...).depth == midFieldUseful(distances: [d], ...). Pure, no ARKit. Fails today on five of six distances plus the thermal row; after the fix the only true/true row is 4.5 m with thermalSerious false, and restoring either the unbounded predicate at 1049 or deleting the thermal term re-reddens exactly those rows. verdicts.industrialSolution: Make suspend a real reset of the scheduler and make resume compute rather than replay. Test: testSuspendClearsPerceptionHoldsSoResumeDoesNotImmediatelyReconfigure — t=0 evaluate(person/depth desired) -> (_,true,true); t=1 evaluate(all false) -> still (_,true,true) (hold engaged); suspend(); t=120 resumeConfig(plan: recon true, person false, depth false) must equal (true,false,false) AND the immediately following evaluate at t=120.01 must return the SAME tuple, i.e. produce no change and therefore no second session.run. verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed, converged with STATE-2 from an independent lens, and this is the build's most serious regression. verdicts.industrialSolution: Stop treating the sceneUnderstanding option set as event-driven state and re-derive it every tick from its inputs — this is literally the rule Wave C's ARP-3 ruling established and which the codebase's own comment at 2288-2294 states ('derived state is computed from its inputs each tick, never written inside the branch its own precondition guards'). Add `nonisolated static func wantsSceneOcclusion(occlusionCapable: Bool, pedestrian: Bool, windowModeActive: Bool) -> Bool` — note the signature deliberately contains NO reconstruction/appliedPerception term, so the exit decision cannot be poisoned by a transient perception state — and reconcile options.insert/.remove from it once per tick at the END of updatePowerTier (after the flag is written, so it never reads a stale sibling). setWindowMode and applyRenderPathIfNeeded then only set their own flags and never touch options. Test: testOcclusionOptionSurvivesAGlassExitDuringThermalShedding — replay the field sequence as a table: (capable, ped, window:false) -> true; window ON -> false; recon shed -> false; window OFF while recon still shed -> false; recon restored -> MUST be true. The final row fails against today's call sites and, tellingly, also fails against pre-Wave-D code for the opposite reason (the transit row would wrongly be true with the old capability constant), so the test locks out both regressions at once.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified. perceptionPlan's reconstruction term is `cameraVisible && pedestrian && !thermalCritical` (GeoARSessionManager.swift:1178) and applyPerceptionHysteresis is applied to person (1108-1111) and depth (1112-1115) only — the raw reconstruction value goes straight into setPerception at 1116. ARSessionHolder.cameraDidDisappear calls markCameraHidden() immediately (68-72 → 466-468) but only schedules the pause 5 s later (109-119), and it is suspendSession that cancels the tick (408-409) — so for those five seconds the tick keeps running and the very next iteration (<=400 ms) reaches setPerception with reconstruction=false and fires session.run on a configuration that omits sceneReconstruction (622-624). So a Camera→Map→Camera flip inside the grace costs two full reconfigurations and a mesh rebuild from zero, during which .occlusion is still in the sceneUnderstanding option set (nothing removes it on this path) and content therefore draws over the wall and the parked car for the whole rebuild — which is the SWE-11 harm verbatim, on the app's most frequent navigation. verdicts.industrialSolution: Give the stable axis a visibility grace, and only the stable axis. Keep `lastCameraVisibleAt` in the manager and pass `cameraRecentlyVisible = Date().timeIntervalSince(lastCameraVisibleAt) < AppConfig.pauseGraceSeconds` into perceptionPlan as a NEW parameter used only in the reconstruction term — person and depth keep raw cameraVisible, since they are per-frame ML whose cost is real the instant the surface is gone. Test: testReconstructionSurvivesATabFlipInsideThePauseGrace — (cameraVisible:false, cameraRecentlyVisible:true) -> reconstruction TRUE; (false, false) -> FALSE; and in BOTH rows person and depth must be FALSE. The third assertion is the load-bearing one: it fails if the fix is applied sloppily by replacing cameraVisible globally, so the test pins both halves and cannot be passed by weakening totality.

verdicts.reasoning: The policy hole is real; the case for changing the policy now is not made, and part of this re-opens a written decision without new evidence. Verified: pickVideoFormat (GeoARSessionManager.swift:687-707) applies `format.fps <= targetFPS` as a hard filter with no second pass, so best stays nil when every in-band format exceeds the target, and makeConfiguration (668-679) then leaves config.videoFormat untouched and marks the HUD UNCAPPED. ARKit's documented default for ARConfiguration.videoFormat is supportedVideoFormats.first, i.e. the device's recommended/highest-throughput entry, so the reviewer is right that the resolution lever is abandoned exactly where the fps lever is unavailable. But: ADR-034 item 1 records this as a DECISION — 'target-fps formats only, smallest resolution >= 720p, else keep ARKit's default' — so proposing a fallback is re-litigating a documented trade, and D5's bar for that is new evidence. Nobody on this team has logged ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.supportedVideoFormats from the iOS-17 device set (deployment target is 17.0, so iPhone XS and later), and I cannot verify from documentation that any of those devices lacks an in-band entry at or below 30 fps. Worse, the proposed test change is a regression in itself: on the fixture [(60,1920x1440),(30,3840x2160)] a lowest-fps-then-smallest-area second pass returns index 0 — which IS ARKit's default — so the behavior is unchanged but the loud UNCAPPED marker and metricsLog.error would be dropped, losing the field evidence for nothing. verdicts.industrialSolution: Sequence it: instrument, then decide. (1) Land the cheap half now — cache the picked index and description on first computation so setPerception does not rescan and republish per reconfiguration, and add a one-time metricsLog.log of the FULL supportedVideoFormats list at attach. That single log line answers the reachability question from the field within one test cycle and costs nothing. (2) If the logs show any shipping device with no in-band format at or below the target, then make the policy two-stage inside pickVideoFormat: first pass unchanged; if nil, second pass over the same area bounds selecting LOWEST fps then SMALLEST area, returned through a distinct result (e.g. `enum FormatChoice { case satisfied(Int), fpsUncapped(Int), unsatisfiable }`) so the HUD reads 'FPS-UNCAPPED' rather than fully UNCAPPED and the loud log survives. Return unsatisfiable only when nothing is in the area band at all. (3) Do NOT rewrite testNeverSelects4KEvenWhenItIsTheOnly30FPSFormat to assert index 0 with the marker silently dropped — keep the 4K refusal and add testFallsBackToSmallestAreaWhenNoFormatMeetsTheFPSCap as a separate row over [(60,1920x1440),(60,1920x1080),(60,1280x720),(60,3840x2160)] expecting .fpsUncapped(2), paired with an all-out-of-band list [(60,3840x2160),(60,640x480)] that must still return .unsatisfiable so a fix that merely deletes the fps filter goes red.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified and, importantly, Wave D made it MORE reachable — which is exactly the D5 exception. snapNearestDropToGround (GeoARSessionManager.swift:1866-1905) runs a truth chain: ARKit estimated-plane raycast, then arView.scene.raycast with mask .sceneUnderstanding, then estimatedGroundY(frame:), then `frame.camera.transform.columns.3.y - 1.65`. The second rung depends entirely on the reconstruction mesh and its collision shapes (requested at 719-722), and the plan can now shed reconstruction on THREE axes — camera hidden, transit (new in Wave D), thermal .critical (1178). ARKit's contract is that scene-reconstruction mesh anchors exist only while the configuration requests .mesh, so with reconstruction shed the mask .sceneUnderstanding raycast has nothing to hit and returns nil silently — an empty result is indistinguishable from 'no surface there'. The chain then falls through to the eye-height guess and the result is committed with adjustNearestDrop(height:commit:true) at 1903, which reaches library.update(persist: true) at 1826, and ground-LOCKED at 1905. groundLockBaseY is authoritative thereafter: it overrides GPS re-sync (1608) and overrides VPS terrain transforms outright (applyVPSTransform, 820-822). No provenance is recorded, so a fabricated height is indistinguishable from a LiDAR measurement forever. The ARScreen 'Place on ground' button (542-551) carries no thermal or render-path gate. Second consumer confirmed: updateWindowMode (1005-1010) probes the same mesh, so with reconstruction shed GLASS mode always resolves off — which is the deterministic trigger for ARPCFG-3, making these two findings a single failure chain rather than two independent ones. The harm is a persistence bug, not just a rendering one: persist: true ships the fabricated height to Firestore where every recipient of the shared link renders the drop buried or floating, and the user's own later GPS/VPS corrections are forbidden from healing it.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Return provenance from the truth chain instead of a bare Float. `enum GroundEstimate { case planeRaycast(Float), mesh(Float), planeAnchor(Float), assumedEyeHeight(Float) }` produced by `nonisolated static func resolveGround(planeHit: Float?, meshHit: Float?, planeAnchorY: Float?, cameraY: Float) -> GroundEstimate`. Only the first three set groundLockBaseY and pass persist: true; .assumedEyeHeight applies the visual move but must NOT lock and must NOT persist, and should surface through showPersistError (93) as 'Couldn't find the ground here — move closer and try again'. Independently, skip the mesh rung and the window-mode probe entirely when appliedPerception.reconstruction == false, so the code states its dependency rather than discovering it as an empty result — that also removes the silent coupling into ARPCFG-3. Test: testGroundSnapWithoutRealGeometryNeitherLocksNorPersists — against resolveGround plus a FakeRaycaster double that returns no hits for BOTH the ARKit plane query and the .sceneUnderstanding query (rule 6: the double reproduces the shed-stream FAILURE mode, not only success), assert the result is .assumedEyeHeight, that groundLockBaseY has no entry for the drop, and that the fake DropLibrary recorded ZERO update(persist:true) calls; a companion row with a mesh hit asserts .mesh, a lock entry, and exactly one persisted update, so the test cannot be passed by over-correcting into 'never lock'.

verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed, and it converges with FLOW-8 from the presentation lens. Verified: makeConfiguration guards each request on hardware — reconstruction on ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.supportsSceneReconstruction(.mesh) (622) and depth on supportsFrameSemantics(.sceneDepth) (628-629) — while perceptionPlan (1161-1189) carries capability only for the person leg (supportsCustomPersonOcclusion, 1185) and NONE at all for reconstruction (1178) or the mid-field depth leg (1186, gated only on the AppConfig flag midFieldEnabled). setPerception assigns `appliedPerception = desired` at 751 BEFORE building the configuration, so appliedPerception records the desire, not the configuration. Consequences both verified. On a non-LiDAR iPhone: appliedPerception.reconstruction is true whenever the camera is visible and pedestrian, line 1119 sets occlusionActive = true, and ARScreen.swift:372-374 lights the blue LiDAR chip — on a device where runGPSCompass:715-723 never inserted .occlusion because occlusionCapable was false. Severity MEDIUM is right for the churn; the HUD dishonesty is what makes it worth prioritizing, because it is the instrument the counsel is using to adjudicate draw-over and heat reports on the majority of the install base.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Push the capability terms into the plan so it can only desire what the hardware can deliver: add `supportsSceneReconstruction: Bool` and `supportsSceneDepth: Bool` to perceptionPlan's signature and AND them into the reconstruction and depth terms respectively (the mid-field leg needs supportsSceneDepth in particular, since it is the only leg with no gate today). That makes appliedPerception a faithful record of the running configuration, makes the change-guard at 750 correct by construction (identical configurations now produce identical tuples, so no-op runs disappear), and makes occlusionActive honest without reintroducing the static capability flag Wave D was right to remove. Test: testPlanNeverRequestsAStreamTheHardwareCannotProvide — plan(supportsSceneReconstruction: false) must yield reconstruction FALSE across every other input combination; plan(supportsSceneDepth: false, midFieldServiceable: true, fullTier: true) must yield depth FALSE; and a manager-level assertion that after a full updatePowerTier on simulated non-LiDAR capabilities, occlusionActive == false so the chip stays dark. Crucially, the same table with both capabilities true must reproduce the existing seven WaveDTests rows unchanged, so the fix cannot be passed by simply forcing the terms off.

verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed, and it converges with FLOW-5 from the presentation lens — two independent traces to the same leak, which is the strongest signal in this review after ARPCFG-3. Verified the complete clearer set for editingDropID/liveEditingDrops: commit (GeoARSessionManager.swift:1834-1835), removePerDropState for that id (1406-1407), resetPlacements (781-782), clearRoomDrops for liveEditingDrops only (564), and the dead bail at 1769-1770 (see STATE-4). verdicts.industrialSolution: Extract a `LiveEditRegistry` value type and make abandonment a policy rather than an accident: `mutating func begin(_ id: UUID, at: Date)`, `tick(_ id: UUID, at: Date)`, `commit(_ id: UUID)`, `expire(now: Date) -> [UUID]` with an INACTIVITY window (1.5 s) rather than a gesture-age window, plus `capturedID` and `isLiveEditing`. verdicts.industrialSolution: Identical to ARPCFG-3 and I endorse this lens's framing of the fix as the canonical one: stop edge-toggling arView.environment.sceneUnderstanding.options entirely and re-derive it every tick from `nonisolated static func wantsSceneOcclusion(occlusionCapable:pedestrian:windowModeActive:) -> Bool`, applied at the END of updatePowerTier so it never reads a stale sibling, with setWindowMode and applyRenderPathIfNeeded reduced to setting their own flags. The proof holds: while editingDropID != nil, updateNearest returns at 1418 without writing nearestDrop, and the only other writers of nearestDrop are adjustNearestDrop itself (1779, writing a drop whose id equals the capture) and relocateNearestDrop (1977, same), so `nearestDrop?.id == id` is invariantly true whenever the capture is set — the fourth arm at 1768 always yields non-nil and the else block at 1769-1770 can never execute. This is the only finding in the set with cloud-data-integrity consequences: a drop the user deleted reappears in the published library, on disk, and in Firestore.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified, and confirmed Wave-D-introduced by git: 2a0f146's RootView.swift contains no scenePhase handler at all (grep for scenePhase returns nothing), so the listener previously survived backgrounding. The re-attached listener's first callback hits `guard self.primedListeners.contains(key) else { self.primedListeners.insert(key); return }` (153-156) and returns without toasting, and because the query is `.order(by: "at", descending: true).limit(to: 1)` (136) that swallowed initial snapshot IS the newest reaction — i.e. exactly the one that arrived while the app was backgrounded. Firestore's contract makes the pre-Wave-D behavior the correct baseline: a snapshot listener that stays registered across a suspension reconnects and delivers documents it has not yet seen as .added document changes against its existing local view, so the toast fired on return; a listener that is torn down and re-added starts a NEW local view whose first snapshot is by definition a full initial state, not a change set — which is precisely why the primed-watermark exists and precisely why clearing it on stop() destroys the delivery. I verified there is no alternative surface: incoming/incomingDropTitle (RootView.swift:139-146) is the only sender-side one, reactions(for:) is the viewer's Memory recap reached only from MemoryScreen, and grep for Messaging/UNUserNotification/remoteNotification across the target returns nothing — no push channel exists. And because the watermark is re-primed on every foreground, the row is history forever, not just this session.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Make the watermark durable rather than per-listener-instance. Persist the last-seen reaction document id (or its `at` timestamp) per drop key in UserDefaults across stop(), and on re-attach toast any initial-snapshot row whose document id differs from the persisted one — that restores delivery without reintroducing the 'toast the whole initial snapshot' bug the watermark was built to prevent. Note the Firestore local cache actually helps here: after re-attach the SDK serves the cached view first and then the server delta, so keying on document identity rather than on snapshot ordinality is the robust discriminator. Secondary: add a deinit to ReactionService that calls stop(), since FIRListenerRegistration does not detach on dealloc and a destroyed scene would otherwise leak live, billed streams — the 'no deinit needed for a process-lifetime root StateObject' judgment is fine for today's single-WindowGroup app but costs one line to make unconditional. Test: ReactionDeliveryTests.testReactionArrivingWhileBackgroundedIsToastedOnReturn with a FakeReactionBackend that reproduces production's SUSPENSION mode per Wave C rule 6 — emits an initial snapshot on every attach containing the newest row, emits later rows as .added, and models stop() as a hard detach. Sequence: attach, emit R0 in the initial snapshot, assert incoming == nil; emit R1 live, assert incoming == R1; stop(); emit R2 while detached; re-attach; assert incoming == R2. A second case with NO new row since teardown must produce incoming == nil — that case passes vacuously today and is what stops the naive fix, so both are required.

One caveat I could not close: I cannot verify from ARCore's published iOS documentation that GARStreetscapeGeometry.mesh vertex pointers remain valid off the main thread for as long as the geometry is retained. verdicts.reasoning: The structural claim is CONFIRMED; the asserted failure is not evidenced. Verified: RootView still carries two presentation modifiers on the same view — .fullScreenCover(item: destinationBinding) at 60 and .sheet(item: $receiveDropID) at 115 — and ReceiveScreen.swift:117-120 runs `onReveal(drop); dismiss()` in one closure, where onReveal's last statement is router.showCamera = true (RootView.swift:134 -> AppRouter.swift:46-51 -> destination = .camera). So one synchronous transaction both requests a fullScreenCover and dismisses the sheet currently presented from the same presenter, and AppRouter's own comment at 20-27 declares this shape unsupported. That is a real residual of SWE-7's stated charter and worth closing. What I will not ratify is the harm as written. Since iOS 14.5 SwiftUI supports multiple presentation modifiers on one view, and the modern presentation coordinator serialises a dismiss followed by a present on the same host rather than dropping the second — the classic 'dropped cover' failure is the case where two presentations are requested SIMULTANEOUSLY, which is not what happens here (the sheet is going away, the cover is arriving). I found no evidence in the repo of the described symptom (user returned to Home with reactionSession.phase == .watching and no AR surface), and the finding presents a UIKit-era rule as if it were current behavior. Note too that the reviewer's own harm narrative depends on the cover being dropped, which would also have been the pre-Wave-D behavior — so this is not a Wave D regression either way. Real anti-pattern, speculative failure, MEDIUM not HIGH.

So: a real structural gap with a trivial fix, worth landing, but not the 'hard-stop UX trap on the acquisition path' the finding claims. LOW/MEDIUM, not HIGH.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Land the fix anyway because it costs one line and removes a whole class: move the dismiss control out of the branch and attach it as `.overlay(alignment: .topLeading)` on the ZStack so it renders in every state, and place it ABOVE revealOverlay in the composite order so the 1.6 s reveal cannot swallow it. Separately, make the arView race self-heal rather than relying on it being unreachable: have ARScreenContent observe holder.arView (it is already @Published) or retry holder.cameraDidAppear() from an .onChange, so a lost configure race resolves itself instead of presenting black forever. Test: testCameraCoverAlwaysOffersAnEscape — an XCUITest matrix over the three states injected by launch argument (-arUnsupported 1, -arViewUnavailable 1, normal), asserting a hittable element with accessibility identifier `camera.dismiss` exists within 2 s in every case and that tapping it returns to the tab bar, plus a sub-assertion that the control is hittable while the reveal overlay is on screen. Cases (a) and (b) time out today; the reveal sub-assertion fails today and is the one with genuine shipping-device reachability.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified, and it falsifies a specific claim in the Wave D build record. videoFormatDescription — the only carrier of the '· UNCAPPED' marker (GeoARSessionManager.swift:672-679) — is rendered only as the tail of metricsLine(ttfo:) (ARScreen.swift:623-629), and that line is gated at 446 on `if let ttfo = manager.timeToFirstObjectMs`. timeToFirstObjectMs is nil unless content is actually placed: markCameraVisible sets 0 only when !placedHolders.isEmpty and otherwise explicitly nils it (474-480), and recordTTFOIfNeeded requires !placedHolders.isEmpty (2024-2028). The whole HUD is additionally removed by a stray viewfinder tap (hudHidden, ARScreen.swift:110-118). So the charter's claim that 'the HUD carries the field evidence' for ARP-6 is false in exactly the sessions that matter: a device on which the format policy is unsatisfiable runs ARKit's platform default and says nothing at all whenever the user opens the camera somewhere with no drops — the first-run Playground, an empty neighbourhood, or a field test that never localizes. ADR-030 calls capture the single biggest heat lever and ADR-034 records the 4K@30 regression that this marker exists to catch, so conditioning that evidence on an unrelated killer-#1 metric is a real instrumentation defect, not a cosmetic one. It also interacts with ARPCFG-5: the reachability question there ('does any shipping device actually hit the unsatisfiable branch?') cannot be answered from the field while the evidence is invisible.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Render the format as its own chip in statusCard alongside LiDAR/SEM/DPT (ARScreen.swift:360-400), tinted red when the description contains 'UNCAPPED', unconditional on timeToFirstObjectMs; leave the metrics line as-is so the existing FT traces keep their shape. Pair it with ARPCFG-5's suggestion to log the FULL supportedVideoFormats list once at attach — between the chip and the log, the unsatisfiable-device question becomes answerable from one field session instead of never. Test: testFormatEvidenceIsVisibleWithoutAnyPlacedContent — unit half asserts a pure `formatChip(description:)` returns a non-nil chip with .uncapped styling for '3840×2160@60 · UNCAPPED'; XCUITest half launches with -forceUncappedFormat 1 and -noDropsNearby 1, opens the camera, and asserts an element whose label contains 'UNCAPPED' is visible within 5 s WHILE timeToFirstObjectMs is still nil (assert the 'first object:' string is absent, proving the metrics line did not render and the chip is carrying it independently). Fails today because no matching element exists.

verdicts.reasoning: Same defect as ARPCFG-7, found independently from the presentation/HUD-honesty lens, and this trace adds the part that makes it matter to the counsel's own process. Verified: perceptionPlan's reconstruction term (GeoARSessionManager.swift:1178) has no capability term; setPerception stores appliedPerception = desired at 751 unconditionally even though makeConfiguration drops the stream unless supportsSceneReconstruction(.mesh) (622); occlusionActive = appliedPerception.reconstruction at 1119; and ARScreen.swift:372-374 renders chip("LiDAR", color: .blue) from it. So on an iPhone 15/16 non-Pro or SE — the majority of the install base — the HUD asserts LiDAR occlusion is active whenever the camera is up in pedestrian mode, on hardware where runGPSCompass:715-723 never inserted .occlusion at all because occlusionCapable was false. This lens also correctly catches that the Wave D build record's own claim ('the pedestrian render-path branch re-inserts .occlusion from device capability') is only half true: 1372-1375 was re-keyed to capability, but 1032 still keys on occlusionActive — which is the ARPCFG-3/STATE-2 regression, so FLOW-8 and ARPCFG-3 are the two halves of one incomplete migration. The instrumentation harm is the one worth stating plainly: the counsel and the field testers adjudicate the BRIEF's zero-draw-over-known-front-surface bar against this chip, so a genuine occlusion failure on non-LiDAR hardware currently reads as 'LiDAR was on, must be a shader bug' and sends the investigation at the Metal pass instead of at the device class.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Fix at the source, exactly as ARPCFG-7 specifies: add supportsSceneReconstruction and supportsSceneDepth to perceptionPlan and AND them into the reconstruction and depth terms, so appliedPerception can never claim an unapplied stream and the change-guard at 750 becomes correct by construction. Belt-and-braces at the display layer only if you want defence in depth: occlusionActive = appliedPerception.reconstruction && ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.supportsSceneReconstruction(.mesh). Do NOT fix this at line 1119 alone — that leaves appliedPerception itself lying to every other downstream consumer, which is the underlying defect. Test: the invariant test is the valuable one and it belongs in the suite permanently — for every (reconstruction, person, depth) triple, assert `appliedPerception.reconstruction implies the produced ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.sceneReconstruction == .mesh`, and the symmetric implication for depth and .sceneDepth. On non-LiDAR simulated capabilities that implication is violated today, and it is the assertion that would have caught this during the build.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified, and it compounds STATE-6 into a two-sided delivery failure. The toast is `.overlay(alignment: .top)` applied to the ZStack holding `screen` + NightTabBar (RootView.swift:44-49, 138-163). SwiftUI/UIKit's presentation contract settles this without ambiguity: a fullScreenCover is presented in its own presentation context above the entire window content, so no modifier applied to the presenting view's own body — overlay, zIndex, or otherwise — can render above it. So the toast is beneath every cover. Worse, its `.task` still runs while covered (the view remains in the hierarchy, merely occluded) and calls reactionService.clearIncoming() after 4 s (158-161 -> ReactionService.swift:213-214), and there is no unread store — so the reaction is not merely delayed, it is destroyed. The same placement and the same consequence apply to the persist-error banner at 169-186, which round 4 added specifically as the 'global backstop' because failures raised from the Map or the receive flow were invisible: it is not global, and a persist failure during the create ritual or the receive redeem can be shown to nobody (only ARScreen's own persistErrorText at 407-412 survives, and only in the camera). Combined with STATE-6 the sender-side reciprocity beat now fails in both of its two most common timings — reacted-while-backgrounded and reacted-while-the-sender-is-in-a-cover.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Two changes. (1) Stop the destruction: suppress the 4 s auto-clear while router.destination != nil (guard the .task on a `deliverable` predicate, or move the timer to fire only when the stage is clear), so a covered toast is queued rather than consumed. (2) Hoist the presentation: either attach both overlays inside each destination's content as well as on the root, or — cleaner and the standard iOS approach for window-level chrome — present them from a separate UIWindow at a higher windowLevel, or use SwiftUI's `.alert`/`.overlay` on the presented content via an EnvironmentObject-driven modifier applied in each cover branch. The persist banner in particular should be a single reusable modifier applied to every full-screen destination, which also removes the duplication with ARScreen's own persistErrorText. Test: testIncomingReactionSurvivesAndSurfacesAfterACoverIsDismissed — XCUITest with a stubbed ReactionService: present the camera destination, inject an incoming reaction, wait 6 s (past the auto-clear), dismiss the camera, assert the 'reacted' toast is visible within 1 s. Unit companion: assert clearIncoming() is not invoked while the suppression flag is set and that the pending reaction is still readable afterwards. Both fail today — after dismissal reactionService.incoming is already nil.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified and it is the simplest real bug in the review. HomeScreen.forYouCard (HomeScreen.swift:145-147) builds a Button over a specific received `drop` but its entire action is `router.showCamera = true` — it never calls reactionSession.startWatching(drop). The link path does both (RootView.swift:133-134). ReactionOverlay is gated on reactionSession.drop != nil (ARScreen.swift:26-30), and phase stays .idle, so no reaction bar, no wrap timer, no Memory. I checked the sibling call sites the finding cites as correctly shaped: the Playground card and the Map viewfinder button legitimately open a plain viewfinder because they are not tied to a specific received drop. So this is a missing statement, not a design tension. The product consequence is exactly as stated and is worth the counsel's attention because it is invisible in every state-level test: PRODUCT-ROUTE §0's receive -> watch -> react -> memory loop is reachable ONLY from a freshly tapped magic link. Anyone who taps 'Later' on the invitation and comes back via the obvious 'you're here — open the camera →' card (HomeScreen.swift:174-180) can see the drop but cannot react, the sender is never told it was opened, and no Memory is produced. Not a Wave D regression, but it sits squarely inside the surface SWE-7 rewrote and is a one-line fix.
verdicts.industrialSolution: `reactionSession.startWatching(drop); router.showCamera = true` in the card's action — drop is already in scope and startWatching already handles token bumping and snapshot reset (ReactionSession.swift:28-36). Then audit for other 'watch this received drop' entry points and route them all through one method rather than two statements at each site: add `func openReceivedDrop(_ drop: GeoDrop)` to the router (or a small view model) that does both, so a third entry point cannot be added with only half the behavior — which is exactly how this one arose. Test: testWaitingForYouCardStartsTheWatchSession — unit half asserts openReceivedDrop(drop) leaves reactionSession.phase == .watching and reactionSession.drop?.id == drop.id; XCUITest half seeds the library with one received drop, launches to Home, taps the card, and asserts the ReactionOverlay 'LIVE' pill and at least one reaction button exist. Fails today because reactionSession.drop stays nil so ReactionOverlay is never rendered.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified and it is the meta-finding that explains how FLOW-1 shipped as CLOSED. AppRouterDestinationTests (WaveDTests.swift:139-190) constructs a bare AppRouter and asserts destination/onboardingPhase after direct method calls — five tests, all pure enum assignment. Every mechanism SWE-7 was chartered to protect lives in RootView and is untested: the two-modifier interleaving (60 vs 115), the queue/promote machine (100-114), the phase→memory rule (94-96), and the identity swaps on a LIVE cover. Wave C binding rule 6 is the exact authority: doubles must reproduce production's isolation, suspension AND failure modes, and the double here is an enum assignment — it has no presenter, cannot suspend mid-dismissal, and cannot drop a presentation. I confirmed the consequence directly: FLOW-1 is a 100%-reproducible first-run break and the entire five-test suite passes against it unchanged, because the router state transition IS correct — it is the view state destroyed by the transition that is the bug, and no router-level test can see @State. The same is true of FLOW-2, FLOW-3 and FLOW-4. So the wave's headline evidence (18 new tests, 130/130 green) reads as coverage of the presentation fix while covering none of it. That is the finding.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Split the problem: make the policy pure and testable, then buy one thin layer of real presentation coverage. (1) Extract every presentation decision into pure router methods — linkArrived(_:coverUp:receiveUp:), promotePendingReceive(coverUp:receiveUp:), memoryBecameReady(cameraUp:), cameraDismissed(watching:), and onboardingBeat as @Published state — and table-test them as a state machine covering the full transition table (story→camera→story preserves the beat; link-while-cover queues and promotes exactly once; link-while-receive-sheet promotes on sheet close; memory presents only when the camera is up; camera dismissal ends a live watch; create is never replaced by memory). Each row fails against current behavior and passes only after FLOW-1..4 are fixed, while the existing five tests stay green throughout — which is itself the demonstration that the shipped suite has no power over this class. (2) Add exactly two XCUITests, not a suite: the onboarding walk-through (Show me → Light fireworks → Magical continue → assert the name beat) and deep-link-while-camera-open (assert the invitation actually appears). Two UI tests is the right amount of expensive coverage for the two flows whose failure is unrecoverable for the user; everything else should be pure. Wire both into the device suite so the 130/130 number starts meaning something about presentation.
